report:
**Conclusion: No—reliable evidence does not show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.**

Early small studies and meta-analyses sometimes suggested benefit, but many were small, poorly controlled, or at risk of bias; results from such studies can be misleading, especially when deaths are uncommon. Better-designed, larger randomized placebo-controlled trials—the most dependable way to test whether a drug prevents death—have not found meaningful clinical benefit.

For example, the large TOGETHER outpatient trial found ivermectin did not reduce COVID-19 hospitalization or prolonged emergency observation, and reported no clinical benefit. The ACTIV-6 trial tested an even higher dose for six days and found no improvement in recovery; its conclusion does not support ivermectin for mild-to-moderate COVID-19. These trials were not primarily powered to detect small differences in mortality because deaths in outpatient populations were rare, but they provide no credible signal that ivermectin prevents progression or death.

A Cochrane systematic review assessed mortality among its key outcomes and rated the evidence using a formal certainty framework; the early evidence base was insufficient/uncertain rather than proof of mortality benefit. That distinction matters: “some studies reported fewer deaths” is not the same as a demonstrated causal reduction in deaths.

Ivermectin remains useful for certain parasitic infections, but the FDA has not authorized or approved it to prevent or treat COVID-19. Avoid animal formulations and self-treatment; excessive doses can cause serious toxicity. For someone at high risk with current COVID-19, a clinician can advise on proven antiviral options promptly.
